segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days John the Baptist came, proclaiming in the wilderness of Judea

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, who said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John himself wore clothing of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region around the Jordan were going out to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So produce fruit worthy of turning back,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The axe is already lying at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I baptize you in water for turning back, but the one coming after me is stronger than I am; I am not fit to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clean out his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the storehouse, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But John tried to stop him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Allow it for now, for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he allowed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After being baptized, Jesus immediately came up from the water; and look, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a voice from the heavens, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I delight.”

notes.note: The traditional 'repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the Hebrew prophets' call to 'return' to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

Matthew's phrase has a plural, 'the heavens', a Semitic turn of phrase that most translations flatten to 'heaven'; it is kept here. The word rendered 'kingdom' leans toward the activity of reigning more than a territory, so the phrase means roughly 'God's reign'. Some translators render it 'reign' or 'rule'.

The Greek perfect tense describes something that has drawn near and now stands close. Scholars dispute whether the sense is 'is about to arrive' or 'has in effect arrived'. The rendering keeps the verb's ordinary meaning of approach and leaves that question open.

notes.phrase: A voice of one crying out in the wilderness
notes.traditional: The voice of one crying in the wilderness
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:3 in the form of the Greek Septuagint, where 'in the wilderness' goes with the voice. In the Hebrew text it more naturally goes with what follows: 'In the wilderness prepare the way.' In Isaiah 'the Lord' is Israel's God, whose return to his people the prophet announces.

notes.phrase: a leather belt around his waist
notes.traditional: a leather girdle about his loins
notes.note: The description echoes that of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have caught the hint that John comes in Elijah's role. Matthew makes the identification explicit later in the Gospel.

The Greek can mean that they were coming to be baptized or only that they were coming to where John was baptizing, perhaps to observe. Most interpreters take it as coming for baptism, which fits John's question about fleeing the coming wrath. The rendering leaves both possibilities open, as the Greek does.

The Greek preposition can mean 'in' (the element into which someone is plunged) or 'with' (the means used), and translations are divided. 'In' is chosen because the verb ordinarily meant to dip or immerse. The same preposition governs 'the Holy Spirit and fire' later in the verse.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God's action to set things right. Here it most likely means doing all that God requires, though some scholars see a reference to God's saving plan.

notes.traditional: the heavens were opened unto him
notes.note: Many manuscripts add 'to him' after 'were opened', which would make the opening of the heavens something Jesus in particular saw. Important early witnesses lack the words, and the Greek text followed here omits them.

The Greek reads literally 'my Son, the beloved', which can be taken as a simple adjective ('my beloved Son') or as a second title. In the Septuagint 'beloved' is sometimes used of an only child. The declaration is widely thought to echo Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1.

candidates.reason: The ordinary sense was 'dip, immerse'; whether to keep the church term 'baptize' or render 'immerse', and whether the following ἐν is 'in' or 'with', needs one decision across the Gospels, Acts and the letters.
Extremely frequent attention-marker that translations render variously as 'behold', 'look', 'see', 'suddenly' or omit; readers will notice inconsistency across chapters.
The perfect ἤγγικεν in kingdom sayings is theologically loaded ('is at hand', 'has come near', 'has arrived') and recurs in Matthew, Mark, Luke, Romans, James and 1 Peter.
Traditional 'preach' now suggests a sermon in church, while the Greek means a herald's public announcement; the choice recurs throughout the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
Translations vary between 'wilderness', 'desert' and 'deserted place', and the word carries Exodus associations that a consistent rendering would preserve.
